ghazal/sh2#3:
How could a rogue's way match piety and abstinence?
What has listening to a sermon to do with the song of the rubab?
ghazal/sh3#8:
Speak of the minstrel and the wine, and seek less the secret of Time—
for no one has solved, or will solve, this riddle by wisdom.
ghazal/sh4#8:
No wonder, in the heavens, if at Hafez's words
Venus's song should set the Messiah dancing.
ghazal/sh11#1:
Cupbearer, light our cup with the glow of wine;
minstrel, sing: the world's affairs have turned to our desire.
ghazal/sh16#8:
Out of piety, I had never before seen wine or a minstrel—
my longing for the tavern boys threw me into this and that.
ghazal/sh19#8:
Cupbearer, minstrel and wine—all are ready, but
there is no joy without the beloved: where is the beloved?
ghazal/sh22#4:
My heart has slipped out of the veil—where are you, minstrel?
Sing out! For from this mode our affairs come round to a tune.
ghazal/sh22#9:
What instrument was it that minstrel played, in his mode, behind the veil—
that life has passed, and my head is still full of its tune and longing?
ghazal/sh29#8:
Seek no place for advice in the corner of my mind,
for this corner is full of the murmur of harp and rubab.
ghazal/sh30#6:
What mode did the minstrel make, that within the mode of the sama'
he shut the door of tumult on the people of ecstasy?
ghazal/sh34#3:
May the breeze bring you joy in union with the rose, nightingale,
for all through the meadow rings your lover's song.
ghazal/sh34#9:
The song of your gathering would now set the heavens dancing,
for Hafez's sweet-spoken verse is your melody.
ghazal/sh35#3:
Until her lip brings me to my desire, like the reed flute,
all the world's advice is but wind in my ear.
ghazal/sh41#1:
Though wine gives joy and the breeze scatters roses,
drink no wine to the sound of the harp—the censor is sharp.
ghazal/sh43#3:
The rose has not yet unveiled, and already she prepares to leave;
lament, nightingale—the cry of the broken-hearted is sweet.
ghazal/sh46#4:
My ear is wholly on the word of the ney and the melody of the harp;
my eye wholly on the ruby of her lip and the turning of the cup.
ghazal/sh53#2:
If I have no song of the morning harp, no matter—
my dawn lament is my advocate.
ghazal/sh90#8:
So that the minstrels may tell you of my longing,
I send you words and verse, with instrument and tune.
ghazal/sh90#10:
Hafez, the song of our gathering is praise of you—
hurry, for I am sending you a horse and a robe of honour.
ghazal/sh101#10:
Take up no cup, like Hafez, except to the moan of the harp,
for the glad heart is bound to the silken strings of mirth.
ghazal/sh111#9:
Beneath the sword of her sorrow we must go dancing,
for whoever was slain by her came to a good end.
ghazal/sh123#1:
What a marvellous instrument and melody the minstrel of love has—
every strain he strikes finds its way somewhere.
ghazal/sh123#2:
May the world never be empty of lovers' laments,
for it has an air both sweet-toned and joy-giving.
ghazal/sh126#5:
The stooped harp is calling you to revelry—
listen: an elder's counsel can do you no harm.
ghazal/sh133#4:
Where is this minstrel from, who tuned the mode of Iraq,
then struck out the tune of return along the road of Hijaz?
ghazal/sh136#5:
When my cypress-tall beloved enters the sama',
what is the garment of the soul worth, if it cannot be torn like a robe?
ghazal/sh137#5:
So did I burn like a candle that, over me,
the flask wept and the lute lamented.
ghazal/sh138#8:
Minstrel, change the mode and play the road of Iraq,
for by that road my beloved went, and gave me not a thought.
ghazal/sh138#9:
The song of Hafez is that of Iraqi's ghazals (and the mode of Iraq):
who heard this heart-burning road and did not cry out?
ghazal/sh142#3:
Give glad tidings, my heart: once more the minstrel of love
struck up a drunken tune and cured our hangover.
ghazal/sh142#5:
The bud on the bush of my union opened at her breeze;
the sweet-voiced bird rejoiced in song over a petal of the red rose.
ghazal/sh144#2:
Do not be without wine and a minstrel: beneath the arch of the sky
with such a song you can drive sorrow from the heart.
ghazal/sh145#2:
What tune does this mode-knowing minstrel strike,
who brings a familiar song into the midst of the ghazal?
ghazal/sh145#3:
You too, take wine in hand and take the road to the meadow,
for the singing bird has brought forth a sweet-toned music.
ghazal/sh146#5:
At the word of the minstrel and the cupbearer I went out, in season and out—
for by that hard road no messenger brings news but with difficulty.
ghazal/sh147#2:
To the morning minstrels we shall give our torn robes,
for the good news the dawn wind has brought.
ghazal/sh153#3:
Last night in the gathering, when my beloved rose to dance,
she loosed a knot of her tresses and struck the hearts of her friends.
ghazal/sh154#1:
Play a tune on whose music one can heave a sigh;
sing a verse with which one can drain a heavy cup.
ghazal/sh158#5:
I who, night after night, have waylaid the road of piety with daf and harp—
shall I now come to my senses? What a notion!
ghazal/sh163#3:
The dancing of the cypress and the mood of the rose—
not sweet without the voice of the nightingale.
ghazal/sh164#8:
Minstrel, this is a gathering of intimacy: sing ghazal and song.
How long will you keep saying, “it went thus, and it will be thus”?
ghazal/sh165#4:
For God's sake, censor, forgive us the cry of the daf and the ney,
for the instrument of the Law will not go out of tune over this tale.
ghazal/sh169#8:
Venus plays no sweet music now—can her lute have burned?
No one has a taste for drunkenness—what became of the wine-drinkers?
ghazal/sh173#8:
Minstrel, sing a fine ghazal of Hafez's words,
that I may say: the days of my gladness have come back to me.
ghazal/sh174#2:
Strike up again, bird of dawn, the song of David,
for the Solomon of the rose has come back on the wind.
ghazal/sh178#9:
I had a patched cloak that hid a hundred of my faults;
the cloak went in pledge for wine and the minstrel, and the infidel's girdle stayed.
ghazal/sh179#5:
They say the song of Jamshid's gathering was this:
“Bring the cup of wine, for Jam will not remain.”
ghazal/sh181#2:
No need of minstrel or wine—only lift your veil,
for the fire of your face has set me dancing like wild rue on the flame.
ghazal/sh184#5:
Thanks be to God, peace has fallen between her and me;
the Sufis, dancing, raised the cup of thanksgiving.
ghazal/sh185#6:
Dancing to fresh verse and the lament of the ney is sweet,
especially a dance in which one takes a fair beloved's hand.
ghazal/sh186#6:
Minstrel, tune the mode, for no one ever died before his hour;
and whoever does not sing this song is mistaken.
ghazal/sh191#2:
First, with the sound of the pipe and the ney, let her send her message to my heart;
then, over one cup of wine, let her be faithful to me.
ghazal/sh193#5:
We are paupers, yet we long for wine and a minstrel—
alas, if they will not take our woollen cloak in pledge!
ghazal/sh197#6:
When our beloved begins the sama',
the holy ones on the Throne fling up their hands in dance.
ghazal/sh200#1:
Do you know what the harp and the lute are declaring?
“Drink your wine in secret, for they are meting out punishment.”
ghazal/sh202#5:
Cut the tresses of the harp for the death of pure wine,
that the companions may all open their lashes to blood.
ghazal/sh203#6:
The minstrel, out of the pain of love, played a piece
at which the sages of the world strained blood through their lashes.
ghazal/sh215#2:
The tale of love, which has no need of letter or sound,
was there in uproar and tumult with the lament of the daf and the ney.
ghazal/sh219#2:
Drink the morning cup to the lament of the daf and the harp;
kiss the cupbearer's chin to the song of the ney and the lute.
ghazal/sh219#3:
In the season of the rose do not sit without wine, a fair companion and the harp,
for like the span of life it is a week, soon counted.
ghazal/sh219#7:
When the rose mounts the air like Solomon,
at dawn, as the bird comes in with the song of David.
ghazal/sh236#7:
What holds her back is the clamor of the harp and the sweet sleep after the morning cup;
otherwise, if she heard my dawn sigh, she would come back.
ghazal/sh238#4:
There was no harp or rebab, no wine or lute yet,
when the clay of my being was already steeped in rosewater and wine.
ghazal/sh240#1:
The March cloud has risen, the wind of Nowruz blows—
I want money for wine and a minstrel: who will say “it has come”?
ghazal/sh241#2:
In your hour of merriment, remember the sighs and laments of lovers
with the voice and strain of the harp and the chaghana.
ghazal/sh241#3:
When the grace of wine shows itself in the cupbearer's face,
remember lovers with song and ballad.
ghazal/sh243#10:
It is not today that we drink to the sound of the harp;
long ago the dome of the heavens heard this noise.
ghazal/sh244#3:
Rebab and harp say, at the top of their voices:
“Lend the ear of reason to the message of the people of the secret.”
ghazal/sh245#5:
What way was this the minstrel struck within the mode?
For drunk and sober are dancing together.
ghazal/sh252#7:
See our sealed secret, how they told it in tale and tune,
with daf and ney, each time in another bazaar.
ghazal/sh254#1:
Once more from the branch of the straight cypress the patient nightingale
raised its rose-song: may the evil eye keep far from the rose's face.
ghazal/sh254#6:
Drink to the sound of the harp and take no grief; and if anyone
says to you, “do not drink wine,” tell him, “God is Forgiving.”
ghazal/sh256#4:
I long for a good companion and a well-tuned lute,
that I may tell my pain in laments, deep and high.
ghazal/sh257#4:
Play the harp and tune it—what matter if there is no aloeswood?
Take love as my fire, my heart as the aloe, my body as the censer.
ghazal/sh257#5:
Come into the sama', throw the cloak from your head and dance;
otherwise go to your corner and put our cloak on your head.
ghazal/sh258#9:
Venus's ghazal-singing would gain no advantage
in that station where Hafez raises his voice.
ghazal/sh259#7:
It cast the murmur of love through Hijaz and Iraq—
the sound and call of Hafez's ghazals from Shiraz.
ghazal/sh262#6:
So much has the harp said, behind the veil, in secret—
cut off its hair, that it may not grow back.
ghazal/sh267#4:
I, who used to call the counsellors' words a mere tune on the rebab,
have had such a boxing of the ears from separation that this one lesson is enough.
ghazal/sh275#2:
Lay your Sufi raptures and ecstatic claims down before the melody of the harp;
give your rosary and mantle to wine and the wine-drinker.
ghazal/sh276#8:
Who is Hafez, that he should not drink wine without the sound of the lute?
Why should a poor lover need such splendor?
ghazal/sh278#3:
Bring wine, for there is no being safe from the cunning of the sky,
with its harp-playing Venus at her game and its warrior Mars.
ghazal/sh283#3:
To the sound of the harp let us tell those tales
whose concealment set the pot of the breast a-boil.
ghazal/sh286#3:
Then she gave me a cup in whose radiance, up in the sky,
Venus came dancing and, playing the lute, cried, “Drink!”
ghazal/sh286#4:
Keep a smiling lip over a bleeding heart, like the cup—
not, at one blow, to burst into wailing like the harp.
ghazal/sh291#3:
Last night, how sweet it was, the nightingale that sang,
while the rose, on its own branch, was all ears.
ghazal/sh292#4:
See how he goes dancing to the lament of the harp,
he who gave no leave to listen to the sama'.
ghazal/sh293#3:
In the corners of the heavens' pleasure-house of Jamshid,
Venus tunes the arghanun to the strain of the sama'.
ghazal/sh293#4:
The harp comes clamoring: “Where has the denier gone?”
The cup comes roaring with laughter: “Where is the forbidder?”
ghazal/sh296#6:
I sit in a corner, fancying myself pious—and strangely,
from every side some tavern lad plays at me with harp and daf.
ghazal/sh304#6:
King, at your feast the heavens are in dance and sama';
let not the hand of joy let go the hem of this song.
ghazal/sh309#2:
A sugar-mouthed cupbearer and a sweet-spoken minstrel,
a companion of good conduct and a boon friend of good name.
ghazal/sh320#5:
My eye on the cupbearer's face, my ear on the word of the harp—
in this matter I took an omen from eye and ear.
ghazal/sh320#7:
The cupbearer held out the bowl to the sound of this ghazal of mine;
I recited this song, and drank the pure wine.
ghazal/sh324#3:
The minstrel's mode will carry me out of my hands—
alas, if I find no entry behind this veil.
ghazal/sh332#7:
May it be nothing but the account of minstrel and wine,
if my scribe's pen draws any figure.
ghazal/sh333#9:
I heard from Venus's harp, at dawn, the words:
“I am the slave of Hafez, sweet of tongue and voice.”
ghazal/sh335#7:
If, like the harp, you grant my heart no desire in your embrace,
then from your own lips, like the ney, play me one breath.
ghazal/sh336#4:
Sit by my grave with wine and a minstrel,
that at your scent I may rise dancing from the tomb.
ghazal/sh340#9:
If the minstrel of the gathering plays the road of love like this,
Hafez's verse at the hour of sama' will carry off my wits.
ghazal/sh348#6:
I will pour a drop from the cup upon this moving throne;
I will cast the clamor of the harp into this enamel dome.
ghazal/sh350#9:
Hafez has grown weary of drinking wine in secret;
to the sound of lute and ney I will make his secret plain.
ghazal/sh351#2:
Where is the minstrel, that I may spend the whole harvest of my piety and learning
on the harp, the lute and the voice of the ney?
ghazal/sh359#7:
In devotion to her, dancing like a mote,
I will go to the very brim of the shining sun's spring.
ghazal/sh360#3:
So that I may tell what was disclosed to me by this journey on the Way,
I will go to the door of the cloister with lute and cup.
ghazal/sh367#5:
If after a hundred years you pass by my grave,
from my clay will rise, dancing, my rotted bones.
ghazal/sh372#6:
Since the Sufis, by ecstasy and dance, are made the leaders,
we too will lift a hand, with a conjurer's trick.
ghazal/sh373#3:
So that all the recluses may take the morning cup,
let us carry the morning harp to the door of the elder of prayer.
ghazal/sh374#4:
Since a fine lute is at hand, minstrel, strike up a fine song,
that we may sing the ghazal with flung hands, and toss our heads as we stamp.
ghazal/sh376#4:
The heavens, that player of the organ, are a highwayman on the people of skill—
how should we not lament at this grief, why not cry out?
ghazal/sh376#6:
We drink an imagined wine from the tulip's cup—
far be the evil eye—we are entranced without minstrel or wine.
ghazal/sh377#7:
My heart has slipped out of the veil—where is sweet-spoken Hafez,
that we may set a tune to his song and ghazal?
ghazal/sh384#5:
O light of the drunkards' eyes, I am in the very midst of waiting—
play the plaintive harp, or pass the cup around.
ghazal/sh386#6:
Come, and see, from the wrong of these hypocrites,
the flask a heart's blood, and the lute crying out.
ghazal/sh391#7:
I led Hafez's heart off the road with daf and harp and ghazal—
what will be the reward of an ill-famed man like me?
ghazal/sh398#3:
The provision of delight is ruined, and the instrument of mirth is gone;
harp, raise your lament; daf, raise your cry.
ghazal/sh413#8:
Hafez, who put the lovers' minstrel's instrument in tune—
may the field of this banquet never be empty of him.
ghazal/sh415#1:
O messenger of the true, tell the news of our beloved;
tell the rose's state to the song-singing nightingale.
ghazal/sh421#6:
From the uproar and tumult of the sweet-working beauties:
sugar broken, jasmine scattered, the rebab struck.
ghazal/sh428#1:
At dawn, hungover from the night,
I took wine with harp and chaghana.
ghazal/sh428#8:
Companion, minstrel and cupbearer—all of it is He;
the fancy of water and clay along the road is only a pretext.
ghazal/sh430#1:
If you will not drink wine to the voice of the nightingale and the dove,
how shall I cure you? The last remedy is the cautery.
ghazal/sh430#5:
Hoarding a treasury for those who will feast on your inheritance is infidelity—
so say the minstrel and the cupbearer, so rules the fatwa of the daf and ney.
ghazal/sh431#5:
Strike the harp in its mode, O moon of minstrels,
and scrape its string till I cry out because of it.
ghazal/sh431#9:
Hold your tongue a while, Hafez;
hear the tale of the tongueless from the ney.
ghazal/sh432#2:
The praise of her moon-like face does not come out right in the veil;
minstrel, strike up a tune; cupbearer, pour some wine.
ghazal/sh440#8:
To the verse of Hafez of Shiraz they dance and they strut—
the black-eyed beauties of Kashmir and the Turks of Samarkand.
ghazal/sh442#8:
How would Hafez's lament have slipped out of the veil,
had it not been the companion of the dawn-singing birds?
ghazal/sh456#3:
The harp, in its mode, gives you this very counsel; but
the sermon profits you only when you are fit to receive it.
ghazal/sh460#3:
Throw reason into the Zayanda-rud and drink wine
to the rose-song of the young men of Iraq.
ghazal/sh460#6:
Youth comes back to my mind:
the sama' of the harp and the cupbearer's flung hands.
ghazal/sh460#11:
Play, minstrel of the sweet voice and sweet speech,
in Persian verse, the Iraqi strain.
ghazal/sh465#1:
At daybreak I went into the garden to pick a rose;
suddenly the voice of a nightingale came to my ear.
ghazal/sh465#5:
When the nightingale's voice worked upon my heart,
I became such that no endurance remained to me.
ghazal/sh466#4:
I will not tell the ascetic's state to people;
if I tell this tale, it is better told with harp and rebab.
ghazal/sh474#3:
Shake out your tresses and bring the Sufi to stamping and dance,
that from every patch of his frock you may shake out a thousand idols.
ghazal/sh479#4:
Cupbearer, be at hand, for grief lies in ambush for us;
minstrel, hold to this very mode you are playing.
ghazal/sh479#5:
Pour wine, for the harp put its head to my ear and said:
“Pass the time sweetly, and heed this bent old man.”
ghazal/sh479#6:
Cupbearer, by the self-sufficiency of the rogues, pour the wine,
that you may hear from the singer's voice, “He is the Self-Sufficient.”
ghazal/sh486#1:
From the cypress branch, in a Pahlavi rose-song,
the nightingale last night was reciting the lesson of the spiritual stations.
ghazal/sh490#9:
How pleased I was with this saying, which at dawn
a Christian was singing at a tavern door, with daf and ney.
ghazal/sh493#4:
A hundred morning breezes dance here with the chain of her tress—
this is your adversary, heart, so do not go pacing the wind in vain.
ghazal/sh495#8:
Every bird has come to the king's rose garden with its own song—
the nightingale with melody-making, Hafez with ghazal-telling.
ghete/sh9#4:
When, in hope of praising you, Venus turns composer of songs,
may your envier, hearing it, be a companion of sighs and laments.
ghete/sh26#4:
The harp's playing, the tune of revelry, the courtyard of the gathering a place for dancing;
the beloved's mole the heart's grain, the cupbearer's curl the snare on the way.
ghete/sh33#4:
Strike, minstrel, upon the second and third strings
the praise of that moon who has no second in beauty.
robaee/sh39#1:
With a lively, charming beauty and with lute and ney,
a corner, some leisure and a flask of wine.
ghaside/sh2#18:
Within the retreat of the cherubim of the sacred world,
the scratch of your pen is the spiritual sama'.
ghaside/sh2#25:
At dawn, how it pleased me that a nightingale was crying its rose-song
to the bud, and saying in its speech:
ghaside/sh3#3:
The sound of the harp so calls to the morning cup
that even the cloister's elder takes the road to the Magi.
ghaside/sh3#20:
When the minstrel raises the music of our gathering,
now he plays Iraq, now he takes up Isfahan.
saghiname/saghiname#4:
Pour, that I may tell, to the voice of the ney,
when Jamshid was, and when Kavus.
saghiname/saghiname#31:
For when Hafez, drunk, makes his song,
Venus, from her sphere, gives out the voice of the lute.
saghiname/saghiname#32:
Minstrel, where are you? To the rose-call of the lute,
bring to mind that royal song.
saghiname/saghiname#33:
So that I may bring ecstasy to work,
I will come into the dance and play the game of the cloak.
saghiname/saghiname#43:
Minstrel, strike up that new-fashioned song
and tell the companions, to the voice of the lute:
saghiname/saghiname#45:
Minstrel, make the music of merriment;
begin the tale with song and ghazal.
saghiname/saghiname#47:
Minstrel, a melody to the rose-call of the lute—
sing, and strike up the royal song.
saghiname/saghiname#49:
Minstrel, bring a figure out of that veil;
see what the keeper of the curtain said from within.
saghiname/saghiname#50:
Raise the voice of the minstrel so high
that you set the harp-playing Venus dancing.
saghiname/saghiname#52:
Minstrel, put the daf and the harp in tune;
in the fine old way, give out the melody.
saghiname/saghiname#58:
To the drunkards send the glad tidings of a song;
to the friends who have gone send a greeting.
